title: Marginal spectral distributions on regular bipartite unitary orbits
abstract: Fix the spectrum of a bipartite density matrix and randomize its eigenbasis according to Haar measure. We study the probability distributions induced on the spectra of the two marginal states. For arbitrary subsystem dimensions $m$ and $n$, the joint characteristic function of the reduced density matrices is expressed as a Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber integral whose external eigenvalues are the pairwise sums $x_i + y_j$. Repeated external eigenvalues are handled by confluent determinant limits. In the two-qubit case, we derive an explicit alternating-spline formula for the joint density of the two marginal Bloch radii. Its support is the Bravyi-Klyachko compatibility region. We also obtain a compact truncated-power formula for the Bloch-radius density of either individual qubit marginal. In the qubit-qutrit case, we derive a truncated-power formula for the qubit Bloch-radius density and a bivariate spline formula for the joint density of the largest and smallest eigenvalues of the qutrit marginal. The latter two variables determine the full qutrit spectrum because the trace is fixed. The derivations combine confluent HCIZ integrals, distributional Fourier inversion, orbital measures, and the SU(2) and SU(3) derivative principles. The resulting densities are piece-wise polynomial on chambers determined by subset sums of the fixed global eigenvalues, in agreement with the Duistermaat-Heckman description of projected coadjoint-orbit measures.
summary: This theoretical paper calculates the probability distribution of local marginal states ($ho_A, ho_B$) given a fixed global spectrum $ho_{AB}$ by averaging over random unitaries. It employs advanced mathematical machinery, notably the Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber integral, to derive explicit, piecewise polynomial formulas for these joint densities. The results provide deep insights into the geometric constraints (compatibility regions) governing local observables in quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper studies the probability distributions induced on the spectra of the two marginal states ($ho_A, ho_B$) when the global bipartite density matrix ($ho_{AB}$) has a fixed spectrum and its eigenbasis is randomized by the Haar measure.
main_result: Explicit formulas, including alternating-spline and truncated-power forms, are derived for the joint density of the marginal Bloch radii in the two-qubit case, whose support is constrained by the Bravyi-Klyachko compatibility region.
method: The analysis relies on calculating the joint characteristic function using Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber (HCIZ) integrals, connecting the problem to Duistermaat-Heckman measures and piecewise polynomial structures.
model_or_system: The system is a bipartite quantum state $ho_{AB}$ with subsystems $A$ (dimension $m$) and $B$ (dimension $n$). The analysis is performed by fixing the global spectrum $\lambda$ and averaging over random unitaries.
key_observables: Joint density of the two marginal Bloch radii ($p_\lambda(a, b)$), and the joint density of the largest and smallest eigenvalues of one marginal (in the qubit-qutrit case).
important_parameters: The fixed global spectrum $\lambda = (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)$ and the subsystem dimensions $m$ and $n$.
main_assumptions: The global spectrum is assumed to be regular (non-degenerate), with degenerate cases handled via confluent limits of the HCIZ integral.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the support of the joint density $G(x, y)$, and Figure 2 shows the explicit two-qubit Bloch-radius density $p_\lambda(a, b)$ for a specific spectrum $\lambda$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the general framework using HCIZ integrals, derives specific formulas for the two-qubit case (Bloch radii), and extends the methodology to higher dimensions (qubit-qutrit) using spline and power formulas.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools (HCIZ integrals, Duistermaat-Heckman theory) to calculate entanglement-related quantities (marginal state distributions) for quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding quantum correlations.
